extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, grant panelists, and research administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observed practices for academic panelists who evaluate fellowship and grant proposals, describing the criteria they use (e.g., excellence, diversity, institutional context, topic priorities) and how they balance competing goals during deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence (academic quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental criterion is the scholarly excellence of the proposal and applicant — mastery of the field, methodological rigor, originality and promise of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists repeatedly foreground excellence as the core standard; some argue only excellence should be considered. Examples: winning requires mastery of both the conventional field and any interdisciplinary/specialized theory (e.g., feminist theory plus seventeenth‑century literature). Excellence is used both as an initial screening metric and as the benchmark to justify endorsing other diversity‑oriented choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic diversity (race, gender, underrepresented groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of the racial and gender composition of awardees and intentionally promoting underrepresented scholars or topics tied to underrepresented groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some panelists explicitly aim to ensure winners 'reflected some diversity in terms of demographics.' Others do not discuss race explicitly, but may promote underrepresented applicants in later stages (e.g., choosing among 'maybe' category candidates). Panelists of color sometimes prioritize demographic representation; some white panelists opposed explicit racial consideration on principled grounds. Examples and tensions are discussed at length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional diversity / institutional affirmative action
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving extra positive consideration to applicants from underrepresented or less‑resourced institutions to spread awards across different types of universities (geography, public/private, elite/nonelite, teaching load).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers may instruct panels to treat underrepresented institutions as 'one extra plus' but not to let it cancel out clear weaknesses. Panelists apply different standards depending on institution resources and career stage; some 'cut less slack' for applicants from richly resourced schools and more slack for those at hostile or under-resourced locales. There is debate about whether this is fair or effective because institutional affiliation correlates with available capital and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive affirmative action (topic- or field-based preferences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferencing research on neglected or strategically valued topics (e.g., feminist scholarship, non‑Western topics, comparative work) to enlarge the intellectual terrain and remedy historical neglect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some competitions explicitly privilege certain fields (e.g., women’s studies, comparative research). Panelists may promote 'non‑Western subjects' or feminist projects as having been marginalized and therefore meriting extra consideration. Such preferences are sometimes justified on grounds of originality, breadth, or social usefulness but can provoke accusations of lowering standards from opponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological/contextual standards (cognitive contextualism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply standards appropriate to the applicant’s epistemological style and field; avoid imposing one discipline's standards on another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists are encouraged to follow 'cognitive contextualism' by evaluating methods and evidence in light of disciplinary norms (e.g., qualitative vs quantitative, positivist vs constructivist). Failure to do so can produce indirect biases (e.g., disadvantaging qualitative work and thereby disadvantaging scholars who more often do such work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing multiple criteria / combining excellence and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberative practice of tempering excellence with diversity considerations rather than treating one set of criteria as exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists describe it as 'healthy' for competing criteria to be vigorously argued and for members to 'temper your own criteria with consideration of alternative criteria.' Some separate 'real evaluation' (quality) from later negotiated rankings where representation is considered; others integrate the two throughout deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case pragmatic adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Making pragmatic, moment‑by‑moment decisions about how far to trade off academic excellence to achieve diversity or other aims, evaluated on a case‑by‑case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some panelists argue against abstract, blanket transformations of excellence standards and prefer pragmatic decisions: 'How far one strays from academic excellence to meet the other goals, you probably have to do that pragmatically, case by case, moment by moment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating gender bias and attribution biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness and active checking for gendered attribution biases (e.g., women judged more harshly, assertiveness penalized for women, different interpretations of self‑promotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social science research shows reviewers give women lower average scores despite similar productivity. Panelists versed in this literature look for patterns in their own scoring by gender and attend to potential tokenism and same‑group biases. Examples: men seen as more competent; women's assertiveness labeled 'too aggressive'; interview styles differ and can disadvantage women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for career stage, resources, and need (contextual adjustment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust expectations based on the applicant’s career stage and the institutional resources available to them (e.g., giving more credit to achievements from hostile or resource-poor environments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers urge different standards depending on resources and career stage; panelists sometimes 'cut less slack' for applicants at resource-rich institutions and more for those at hostile or under-resourced institutions. Assessing 'need' is typically framed as illegitimate, but tensions persist about whether prior support or resource disparity should influence decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overconcentration / representational logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire to avoid all awards going to a small set of elite institutions or the same cohort repeatedly; distributing awards to reflect the diversity of higher education institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ACLS and some program officers value a distribution of awards across institution types; panelists sometimes feel 'chagrined' when finalists are concentrated among major research universities. This is both a fairness and organizational efficacy concern; some panelists shuffle rankings post‑evaluation to improve representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of prior awards and limiting repeat awardees
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion about whether to limit fellowships for applicants who have previously received them, balancing track record as evidence of excellence vs distributive justice and need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists sometimes suggest limiting repeat recipients but find it sensitive because track record indicates excellence; need is rarely invoked explicitly as a legitimate factor, though the distributional question remains contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview performance and presentation style
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of applicants’ interview skills and presentation style, noting gendered differences in perceived persuasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists report men often interview more persuasively and women may be perceived as less forceful or penalized for assertiveness. Interview style can affect funding decisions and is therefore a relevant criterion that may interact with gender bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative advantage and symbolic cues (affiliation, letters, prestige effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that affiliation with prestigious institutions, prominent mentors, and stronger letters of recommendation confer advantages that can keep proposals 'above the bar' (Matthew effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists acknowledge that being at top institutions or working with well-known advisors provides informational shortcuts and reputational signals that influence judgments. This can disadvantage candidates from lesser‑known institutions even when their work is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separating technical quality scoring from post-hoc representational adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: A two‑stage practice where panelists first score proposals on quality alone, then later 'shuffle' or adjust selections to improve representation across topics/institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some panelists preserve the 'sanctity' of quality assessment by keeping it separate from later negotiated rankings where considerations like representation are explicitly factored in: 'At that level, I’m not judging them on the basis of quality, I’m just judging them on the basis of representation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of topical narrowness or Euro/Americano‑centrism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer proposals demonstrating awareness of intellectual worlds beyond a narrow Euro/American focus; narrowness is treated as a negative signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists value applicants who show breadth (e.g., knowledge beyond Eurocentric frames) and mark down 'pomposity' or sweeping statements based only on European material. This intellectual breadth can be used to justify prioritizing certain proposals.
